crime.value: Planned contract murder / ambush: two armed men take over a desert diner, holding staff and a customer hostage, intending to shoot a fugitive named Spikes as he steps off a passing freight train. Central question is not whodunit but whether the intended killing can be prevented.
crime.quote: “We’re going to kill a man named Spikes,” Earl told him.

victim.value: Spikes, a fugitive hiding in a boxcar expecting a getaway car and a friend to drive him to Mexico; targeted because he 'did something he shouldn't have done' — apparently betrayed his associates. Secondary victims: the hostages who could identify the gunmen.
victim.quote: “Let’s just say he did something he shouldn’t have done,” Frank said.

closed_world.value: Charley's Oasis — an isolated wooden diner/gas station in the lower Arizona desert, alone between the highway and the railroad tracks, forty miles from Yuma; five people sealed inside at gunpoint for twenty minutes before the 5:30 freight.
closed_world.quote: a faded sign, the black-lettered words dulled by the hot desert winds, which read: Charley’s Oasis.

culprit_and_motive.value: Frank (black hair, moustache) and Earl (blond), professional hunters-of-men/hired killers, known from the outset; motive is retribution on behalf of whoever Spikes wronged, luring him with a promised escape car that will never come.
culprit_and_motive.quote: “We’re hunters,” the other man said, smiling. ... “There’s some good hunting right here.”

resolution.value: Order restored by improvised action, not deduction: the old man signals Jack toward a gun hidden in rags under the register, hurls scalding coffee at Frank while Jack shouts a warning and shoots Earl in the shoulder; Mandy phones the sheriff, who arrives with deputies and an ambulance. Spikes flees; Jack finds moral resolution and goes home.
resolution.quote: “Mandy,” he said to the girl, “call the sheriff.”

investigator.value: Jack Hennessy, a 31-year-old penniless drifter riding freight trains, fleeing his wife Karen and himself — an outsider bystander whose viewpoint frames the events and who becomes the reluctant agent of rescue.
investigator.quote: He saw a man named Jack Hennessy, a man who was thirty-one years old, and who looked forty.

suspect_architecture.value: No whodunit cast; the antagonists are known from the outset — two armed killers, Frank (dark-haired, moustached, the leader) and Earl (blond, talkative), against three hostages: drifter Jack Hennessy, the old man (Poppa), and his teenage daughter Mandy.
suspect_architecture.quote: Frank, the one with the black hair and moustache, said, “You, old man, come out here.”

red_herring.value: The two gunmen present themselves as ordinary travellers and then as 'hunters,' letting the girl and Jack misread their menace as joking or drunkenness before the guns appear.
red_herring.quote: “We’re hunters,” the other man said, smiling.

clue_fairness.value: Fair-play staging of the escape: the hot coffee pot on the two-burner and the gun wrapped in rags on the shelf beneath the register are both described to the reader before they are used.
clue_fairness.quote: It was wrapped in the rags on the shelf, so that only the tip of the barrel showed.

social_world.value: Marginal desert roadside economy — a family-run diner (Poppa and daughter) forty miles from Yuma, transient freight-riders shooed off by siding men threatening the sheriff, and organised killers moving contraband men to Mexico.
social_world.quote: the man at the siding told him that the sheriff would be called if he stayed around there

alibi.value: No alibi structure; instead Jack tells reflexive lies about himself (broken-down car, waiting friend, Boston origin) that function as a false personal cover story.
alibi.quote: “My car broke down,” he said, and then wondered why he had lied.

reveal_mechanic.value: Demonstration by action and mirroring: the ambush is defeated by the coordinated coffee-pot/gun gambit, and Jack's self-knowledge is revealed when he watches the intended victim flee and recognises himself in the running man.
reveal_mechanic.quote: That’s me running, he thought with a sudden realization

media_and_audience.value: Minimal; official framing arrives only with the sheriff's routine questions, and the story ends with the sheriff smiling in incomprehension at Jack's meaning.
media_and_audience.quote: The sheriff just smiled, because he did not understand.

investigator_wound.value: Jack Hennessy's flight from Karen and from himself — four months of drifting, lying, and self-punishing poverty; the hostage crisis forces him to choose to act and ends his running.
investigator_wound.quote: Oh, why do I have to keep thinking about her? How long will it go on? Aren’t you ever able to forget?

victims_enemies.value: Spikes, the man on the freight, is targeted by two hired killers, Frank and Earl, who arrive ahead of him at the diner; they say only that he 'did something he shouldn't have done,' implying a betrayal of criminal associates — including the 'friend' who was supposed to drive him to Mexico but set him up instead.
victims_enemies.quote: “Let’s just say he did something he shouldn’t have done,” Frank said.

suspect_wounds.value: Jack Hennessy's wound is not guilt of a crime but self-inflicted flight: a thirty-one-year-old who looks forty, penniless, riding freights, compulsively lying to strangers, running from his wife Karen and from himself. The hostage crisis activates exactly this vulnerability — forcing him to choose action over flight.
suspect_wounds.quote: “My car broke down,” he said, and then wondered why he had lied.

unreliable_frame.value: Jack is the unreliable center: a compulsive, unmotivated liar about his car, his destination, his origin ('Boston'), whose reasons for leaving Karen are withheld from the reader; the killers also lie, promising the hostages they won't be harmed.
unreliable_frame.quote: Still another lie. They seemed to flow from his lips without conscious thought.

setting_as_constraint.value: Charley's Oasis, an isolated desert diner between the highway and the railroad tracks, forty miles from Yuma with no other people and no traffic — the killers exploit this isolation and the fixed schedule of the 5:30 freight, whose slowing near the siding makes it the only place Spikes can jump off and the only building he can walk to.
setting_as_constraint.quote: “At five-thirty that freight is coming through here. There’s a man named Spikes hiding in one of the boxcars”

evidence_type.value: No investigative evidence — the case resolves through physical action and eyewitness testimony given to the sheriff afterward; the decisive 'evidence' is environmental/physical: the hidden revolver wrapped in rags on the shelf beneath the cash register and the glass coffee pot on the two-burner.
evidence_type.quote: It was wrapped in the rags on the shelf, so that only the tip of the barrel showed.

false_suspect.value: Jack himself is framed by circumstance as a suspicious figure — thrown off a freight, beard-stubbled, filthy, penniless, lying about who he is — the drifter the man at the siding threatened with the sheriff and county jail; the fleeing Spikes at the end is the other man who 'looks guilty' by running.
false_suspect.quote: the man at the siding told him that the sheriff would be called if he stayed around there

technical_detail.value: Jack's Army firearms training — ten years unused — supplies the reflex that makes the counterattack work: his finger automatically slides the safety off as he snatches the concealed gun, and the coordinated timing of the scalding coffee pot throw jerks Earl's shot into the wall.
technical_detail.quote: his finger automatically sliding off the safety the way he had been taught in the Army

moral_ambiguity.value: Jack, the sympathetic 'culprit' of his own ruined life, isn't wicked but wounded — he fled believing he was sparing Karen pain, and realizes the only person he was hurting was himself; conversely he must shoot a man to save strangers, and takes no pleasure in it.
moral_ambiguity.quote: I thought I was hurting Karen, but in reality the only person I had been hurting was myself.
